title: One pass, one card home for good
hook: Can a single card be in its final sorted place before anything else is sorted?

doesNotKnow: that one partition pass fixes the pivot's final position
that quicksort is partitioning repeated on each pile

misconception: Sorting must compare everything before anything is in its final place.
objective: The learner can explain that after one partition the pivot sits at the position equal to the number of smaller items (5 lands at position 3 in [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7]) and never moves again, leaving two independent smaller piles.

claims.text: Partitioning [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7] around 5 puts 5 at position 3, counting from 0.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: smaller cards fill from the left, larger from the right, pivot drops into the gap; SMALLER = 3 (2, 1, 3). Builder recomputed in Node: count of values below 5 = 3.

claims.text: After partitioning, the pivot's position equals the number of smaller items, which is also its position in the fully sorted row, so it never moves again.
claims.source: In sorted order (distinct values) exactly the smaller items precede the pivot; partition places all of them, and only them, before it. CLRS 3rd ed., 7.1.

claims.text: Nothing in the left pile ever needs to cross the pivot, so each pile is a separate smaller problem; repeating the partition on each pile is quicksort.
claims.source: Hoare, 'Quicksort', The Computer Journal 5(1), 1962; CLRS 3rd ed., 7.1 (QUICKSORT recurses on the two subarrays).

claims.text: On already sorted input, always picking the first card as pivot leaves one pile empty every time, and quicksort slows to about n²/2 comparisons.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., 7.2 (worst-case partitioning, Theta(n^2)); with first-element pivot on sorted input the comparisons are (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2.

claims.text: A pivot that splits the piles evenly makes quicksort fast.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., 7.2 (best-case and balanced partitioning give O(n lg n)); Knuth TAOCP Vol. 3, 5.2.2 (average about 1.39 n lg n comparisons with random pivots).

recall.question: You partition a list of 20 distinct numbers around a pivot, and 12 of them are larger than the pivot. Where does the pivot end up, counting from 0?
recall.why: 19 other numbers, 12 larger, so 7 are smaller. Exactly those 7 come before the pivot, so it sits at position 7, its final sorted place.
